children: What's the most attractive oil stock right now for investors?
Seeking Alpha analysts
, and
offer their picks.

Long Player: Right now, the whole section is rising due to the fast upward push of oil stocks, but at some point quality will again matter. I therefore highly recommend that investors look for quality stocks when investing in oil and gas.

If you are in a junky area of the market (which is roughly a market cap of $300M and under) without a good reason, then it's time to head to industry leaders in case there is demand destruction and possibly a recession, or worse.
I am looking at stocks like ExxonMobil
and the recession-resistant midstream group like Enterprise Products Partners
and Western Midstream
right now.
If you just have to have a fling, consider the Jerry Jones-controlled company of Comstock Resources
, which is now working on a new discovery in the Western Haynesville.
(Long Player leads the SA investing group Oil & Gas Value Research.)
Dhierin Bechai: When looking at integrated oil companies, I previously preferred ExxonMobil
over Chevron

as it could benefit from advantaged asset development, but now I'm leaning more towards Chevron. The reason is that at near-identical EV/EBITDA multiples in my prior analyses on both companies, ExxonMobil
was a hold and only became a buy when implementing a premium multiple.
At current prices both companies likely need a premium multiple, a continued high oil price environment, or a combination of those factors to justify a continued buy rating, but I like Chevron’s
valuation better.
The state of the global economy, however, is increasingly becoming a watch item, as high oil prices are only good for oil companies if demand continues to exist.
(Dhierin Bechai leads the SA investing group The Aerospace Forum.)
Daniel Jones: When it comes to the major oil and gas companies, one of the best has got to be ExxonMobil
In early August, I compared it to competitor Chevron

, and what I found was that future expected growth paved the way for meaningful upside. Management was expecting earnings growth to be $25B between 2024 and 2030, with cash flow growth expected to be $35B. This was not just because of an expansion in output. ExxonMobil is a diversified player in the energy space that has been continuing to focus on high-value products.

The company has also been diversifying into other revenue streams, including its Low Carbon Solutions business for emission reduction opportunities like carbon capture and storage, hydrogen, low-emission fuels, lithium for the global battery and EV market, and so on. In an article that I wrote about the business in December 2025, I pointed out how management expected earnings from these operations to grow to $13B by 2040.
If we focus on the smaller players in the oil patch, one of my top picks has got to be Chord Energy Corporation
. In late August, I analyzed the company. Most of its revenue comes from oil, though the business does have some small exposure to natural gas and natural gas liquids.

Because of elevated energy prices, Chord seemed to be on track to generate free cash flow next year of between $1.13B and $1.39B. And it was trading at an EV to EBITDA multiple of just 2.8 at a time when players in the industry typically trade at between 4 and 6. I even determined that if oil prices were to drop to $60 per barrel next year, the company would still be free cash flow positive.

Although conceptually riskier and less diversified than the major oil-oriented businesses, Chord may have greater upside potential, especially if energy prices remain high. Plus management continues to make interesting moves.

On September 16th, Chord announced that it agreed to sell its entire non-operated Marcellus position in a transaction worth $550M on a gross basis. The goal here is to reduce leverage and focus on core assets. The move also shifts the weighting of the company even more heavily toward oil, with that weight growing by between 4% and 5%. It will also decrease capital expenditures for the business by about $25M on an annual basis.
(Daniel Jones runs the SA investment newsletter Crude Value Insights.)
